en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Familiarity within the Section of Puzzling Questions (Meṇḍakapañha)
3. The Question on the Buddha’s Freedom from Illness “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, I am a brahmin devoted to begging, my hand is always open, I bear my final body, and I am the unsurpassed physician and surgeon.’”
Furthermore, it was said by the Blessed One:
“This is the foremost, monks, among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are free from illness, namely Bākula.
Yet it is seen that illness arose in the Blessed One’s body on many occasions.
“If, venerable Nāgasena, the Tathāgata is unsurpassed, then the statement that ‘Bākula was the foremost among those who are free from illness’ must be false.
If the elder Bākula was the foremost among those who are free from illness, then [the claim] ‘I am... must be false.”
“That he was a surgeon—that statement is also false.
This too is a double-pronged question that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.
“Indeed, Great King, this was also spoken by the Blessed One:”
‘I am... [as before] ...a surgeon,’ and it was said:
‘This is the foremost... [as before] ...’
"Bākulā" means this was said with reference to the fact that he possesses within himself the external scriptures, realizations, and teachings.
Furthermore, Great King, there are disciples of the Blessed One who spend their time day and night standing or walking;
but the Blessed One, Great King, spends his time day and night [in all four postures]: standing, walking, sitting, and lying down.
He passes the time. As for those monks, Great King, who are practitioners of standing and walking meditation, they excel in that respect.
Furthermore, Great King, there are disciples of the Blessed One who eat from a single sitting; even for the sake of their lives, they do not consume a second meal.
Yet the Blessed One, Great King, eats a second meal and even a third.
Those monks, O Great King, who are eaters of a single meal, are superior in that respect.
O Great King, those various reasons have been spoken with reference to this or that particular case.
But the Blessed One, O Great King, is unsurpassed in virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
With reference to the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the eighteen qualities of a Buddha,
and the six unique knowledges, as well as the entire domain of a Buddha, it was said: “I am … [and so forth].”
"A surgeon," [it is said].

"In this world, Great King, among men there is one who is noble by birth, one who is wealthy, one who possesses knowledge, one who possesses craft, one who is brave, and one who is wise; having surpassed all these, the king alone is the highest among them.
Even so, Great King, the Blessed One is the foremost, the eldest, and the best of all beings."
As for the fact that the Venerable Bakkula was free from illness, that was due to his previous resolve. For, O Great King,
when a wind-disorder arose in the stomach of the Blessed One Anomadassi, and when a "grass-flower" disease arose in the Blessed One Vipassī and in six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus,
he himself, being at that time an ascetic, removed that affliction by means of various medicines.
He attained freedom from illness and was declared, “The foremost among those who have attained this is Bākula.
Great King, whether the Blessed One’s illness had arisen or not, and whether he had undertaken the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) or not, there was no being whatsoever equal to the Blessed One.
This was also spoken, O Great King, by the Blessed One, the God above gods, in the distinguished mark of the Saṃyutta Nikāya:
“Bhikkhus, whatever beings there are—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless;
whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata is declared to be the foremost among them.”
“‘He is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One.
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
The third dilemma: On the Buddha’s Freedom from Illness.
